page_hint: Section 5, Common Mistakes, fifth bullet (Overlooking protocol overhead)
quoted_clause: [DERIVED: 64/66 line code plus framing/FEC overhead] attached to '~180 Gb/s' for a '200 Gb/s RoCEv2 link'
observed: The DERIVED label cites 64/66 line code as the derivation basis for the ~180 Gb/s figure, but the same paragraph explicitly states that 200GbE (802.3ck) uses 256b/257b block coding, not 64b/66b. The stated derivation basis contradicts the paragraph's own line-coding claim for 200GbE.
evidence: The paragraph reads: 'Ethernet line coding is named per rate: 200GbE and 400GbE (802.3ck) use 256b/257b block coding before FEC' — then the DERIVED label for ~180 Gb/s says '64/66 line code plus framing/FEC overhead.' 64/66 is the encoding for 802.3bs-defined 200GbE variants (e.g., 200GBASE-CR4), not 802.3ck. If 256/257 + RS(544,514) FEC is used: 200 × 256/257 × 514/544 ≈ 188 Gb/s before framing, ~184 Gb/s after typical RoCEv2 framing — not ~180. If 64/66 is used: 200 × 64/66 ≈ 194 Gb/s before framing, ~188–190 Gb/s after framing — also not ~180 without additional unstated overhead. Either way, the label's stated basis and the paragraph's line-coding claim are inconsistent.
root_cause: The DERIVED label was written for a 64/66-based calculation but the paragraph's line-coding sentence was updated to cite 802.3ck (256/257) without updating the label to match.
correction: Either (a) change the DERIVED label to cite 256/257 block coding (matching the paragraph's 802.3ck claim), recompute with RS(544,514) FEC + framing, and adjust ~180 to the recomputed value (~184 Gb/s); or (b) explicitly scope the 200GbE figure to 802.3bs (64/66) variants and note that 802.3ck variants use 256/257. The NDR InfiniBand ~380 Gb/s figure in the same bullet is correct (400 × 64/66 ≈ 388, minus protocol overhead ≈ 380) and needs no change.
acceptance_test: The DERIVED label's stated line-coding basis matches the paragraph's own claim about which encoding 200GbE uses, and the ~180 Gb/s figure is arithmetically consistent with that stated basis.

quoted_clause: Latency column: '~us' for GPU-to-GPU (NVLink), GPU-to-CPU/NIC (PCIe), Node-to-node (RoCE/Ethernet), and Rack/cluster (InfiniBand) rows
observed: All four network-layer rows show '~us' in the Latency column, making NVLink, PCIe, RoCE/Ethernet, and InfiniBand appear identical in latency. The chapter's opening paragraph claims 'Each layer still has a distinct bandwidth ceiling, a distinct latency profile, and a distinct cost per gigabyte,' but the table's latency column communicates no distinction among network layers.
evidence: Representative latencies: NVLink ~1–2 μs, PCIe ~1–2 μs (DMA-dependent), RoCE/Ethernet ~2–10 μs (hop-dependent), InfiniBand ~1–5 μs (hop-dependent). All are microsecond-class but span roughly an order of magnitude. The bandwidth column clearly differentiates layers (900 GB/s → 64 → 50 → 25 GB/s), but the latency column collapses all network layers to '~us.' The table's stated purpose (per the note below it) is to show hierarchy; the latency column fails to do so.
root_cause: The latency column was populated with a coarse order-of-magnitude label rather than representative ranges that distinguish the layers, despite the chapter claiming distinct latency profiles.
correction: Replace '~us' with representative ranges that distinguish layers: NVLink '~1–2 μs', PCIe '~1–2 μs', RoCE/Ethernet '~2–10 μs', InfiniBand '~1–5 μs', each tagged [ILLUSTRATIVE] if not 1P. Alternatively, add a brief note under the table: 'All network layers are microsecond-class but differ by roughly an order of magnitude; the bandwidth column is the primary differentiator in this table.'
acceptance_test: A reader can see from the table that network-layer latencies differ meaningfully, consistent with the chapter's claim of 'a distinct latency profile' per layer.

quoted_clause: 'If the architecture calls for data-parallel training of a 70B FP16 model across 8 nodes (an eight-rank DP group, e.g. one rank per node), the all-reduce bandwidth dictates whether the nodes are connected by InfiniBand, 200 GbE, or even 100 GbE. If the budget can accommodate NVLink‑equipped hosts (GPUs connected on‑node), keeping the all-reduce on-node gives an ideal ring time about 1/11th the assumed InfiniBand case'
observed: The paragraph opens with an 8-node DP scenario (one rank per node, gradient all-reduce must cross node boundaries) then abruptly shifts to 'keeping the all-reduce on-node' — which can only describe a different deployment: a single-host DP group (8 GPUs on one host). The scenario change is not signaled. A reader may initially interpret 'on-node' as keeping the 8-node DP all-reduce within each node, which is nonsensical for a cross-node DP group. The paragraph then returns to the 8-node scenario ('An eight-node data-parallel job uses NVLink/NVSwitch for intra-node exchanges') without noting that this implies a hybrid TP+DP configuration (TP within each node, DP across nodes) that was never explicitly stated.
evidence: In an 8-node DP group with one rank per node, the gradient all-reduce necessarily crosses node boundaries. 'Keeping the all-reduce on-node' requires 8 GPUs on a single host forming the DP group — a different deployment. The text later clarifies ('The 1/11 and 1/180 ratios compare an eight-rank single-host collective with an eight-rank cross-host collective') but this comes after the potentially confusing sentences. Additionally, 'An eight-node data-parallel job uses NVLink/NVSwitch for intra-node exchanges' implies TP within each node (since pure DP with one rank per node has no intra-node collective exchanges), but the hybrid TP+DP configuration is never explicitly stated.
root_cause: Two distinct deployment scenarios (8-node DP vs single-host DP) are presented in consecutive sentences without an explicit transition, and the hybrid TP+DP configuration assumed by the 8-node scenario is not stated.
correction: Add an explicit transition between scenarios: 'Alternatively, if the eight-rank DP group fits within a single NVLink-equipped host, the all-reduce stays on-node and...' or restructure as a two-option comparison. State the hybrid configuration explicitly: 'In a typical 8-node deployment, each node uses tensor parallelism across its 8 GPUs (NVLink for intra-node activation all-reduces) while data parallelism spans nodes (IB/RoCE for gradient all-reduces).' Move the existing clarification ('The 1/11 and 1/180 ratios compare...') to immediately after the ratios are introduced.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify which deployment scenario each sentence describes without reading ahead to the clarification, and the hybrid TP+DP configuration is explicitly stated where it is first assumed.

quoted_clause: 'each per-layer all-reduce is ~0.45 MB sent per rank — batch × hidden × bytes'
observed: The formula 'batch × hidden × bytes' computes the logical tensor size, but the phrase 'sent per rank' implies physical network traffic. The chapter explicitly distinguishes these in §9.1: 'The 140 GB is a logical input size, not the physical traffic of the collective.' For a ring all-reduce with N ranks, physical send volume per rank is 2(N−1)/N × tensor_size (1.75× for N=8). The mini-case presents the logical size as 'sent per rank,' contradicting the chapter's own terminology distinction. Additionally, the downstream claim 'the tens of MBs... is the per-step total across all 80 layers' is ambiguous: 0.45 × 80 = 36 MB (logical, 1 all-reduce/layer) vs 0.79 × 80 = 63 MB (physical ring, 1/layer) vs 126 MB (physical ring, 2/layer — standard Megatron-style TP has 2 all-reduces per layer: after attention and after MLP). 126 MB is not 'tens of MBs.'
evidence: §9.1: 'The 140 GB is a logical input size, not the physical traffic of the collective. For an eight-rank point-to-point ring, each rank sends 245 GB and receives another 245 GB.' The mini-case's 0.45 MB is batch × hidden × 2 (FP16), which is the tensor size per all-reduce. Physical ring traffic per rank would be 1.75 × 0.45 ≈ 0.79 MB. The number of all-reduces per transformer layer is not stated (standard TP implementations use 2: attention output + MLP output). The canonical batch and hidden size are referenced but not stated inline — 0.45 MB is NOT VERIFIED against the canonical workload definition. The '80 layers' figure is standard for LLaMA-2 70B but NOT VERIFIED against the book's canonical model.
root_cause: The mini-case uses 'sent per rank' to mean 'tensor size per all-reduce' without distinguishing logical from physical traffic (contradicting §9.1), and does not specify how many all-reduce operations occur per transformer layer or whether the total is logical or physical.
correction: Change to 'each per-layer all-reduce operates on a ~0.45 MB tensor (batch × hidden × bytes)' — removing 'sent per rank.' For the total, state the basis explicitly: 'the logical tensor volume across all 80 layers is ~36 MB (1 all-reduce/layer) to ~72 MB (2/layer)' or provide the physical traffic figure with the ring factor stated. Specify the all-reduces-per-layer count. Ensure the basis (logical vs physical) is consistent with §9.1's distinction.
acceptance_test: The mini-case's per-layer figure is labeled as either logical tensor size or physical traffic, consistent with §9.1's terminology; the all-reduces-per-layer count is stated; and the 'tens of MBs' total is derived from a stated basis that arithmetically yields a value in the 'tens of MBs' range.

quoted_clause: 'The team considers replicating an eight-GPU tensor-parallel engine or partitioning one engine across 32 hosts.'
observed: The mini-case presents two alternatives (8-GPU TP replication vs 32-host partitioning) but only requires the reader to reason about the first. The 32-host option is never quantitatively evaluated — no communication volume, latency, or bandwidth calculation is performed for it. The reader is told the answer ('keep TP within a host') without exercising the chapter's arithmetic on the competing option. The chapter's core method — compute bytes, divide by bandwidth, compare to budget — is applied to only one side of the decision.
evidence: The mini-case calculates per-layer TP all-reduce size (~0.45 MB) and KV transfer (~35 GB, ~0.08 s) for the 8-GPU option, but provides no corresponding calculation for the 32-host option (e.g., cross-host activation exchange volume per microbatch, pipeline stage communication cost, or network bandwidth requirement at the stated fabric speeds). The recommendation 'keeping each tensor-parallel engine within an eight-GPU host' follows from explaining why the 8-GPU option's communication is small, not from comparing it to the 32-host option's communication.
root_cause: The mini-case explains why the recommended option is correct rather than requiring the reader to derive the comparison from the chapter's arithmetic.
correction: Add a brief quantitative sketch for the 32-host option: e.g., 'If the model is pipeline-parallel across 32 hosts with S stages, each microbatch sends one stage's activation tensor across the network — at batch B, hidden H, FP16, that is B×H×2 bytes per stage boundary per microbatch, crossing at ~25–50 GB/s. Compare this per-microbatch cross-host cost to the 8-GPU TP option's per-step on-node all-reduce.' The reader should perform or follow this comparison to reach the recommendation.
acceptance_test: The mini-case requires the reader to compute or evaluate communication cost for BOTH alternatives before the recommendation is stated, using the chapter's bytes÷bandwidth method.

page_hint: Section 7, What We Still Don't Know, third bullet (Optical interconnects)
quoted_clause: 'optical intra‑rack fabrics (400 Gb/s–800 Gb/s per lane) are entering data centers'
observed: 'Per lane' is ambiguous (wavelength? electrical lane? fiber pair? module aggregate?) and the upper end (800 Gb/s per lane) overstates current deployment readiness. As of 2026, mainstream optical lane rates are 100–200 Gb/s PAM4; 400 Gb/s per single wavelength/lane is in early development; 800 Gb/s per lane is research-stage. The present-tense 'are entering' implies deployment readiness for the full 400–800 range.
evidence: Current 800G optical modules use 8×100G or 4×200G lanes — the module aggregates to 800 Gb/s but no single lane runs at 800 Gb/s. 400G per single wavelength is not a shipping product. The claim conflates module-level aggregate rates with per-lane rates, or uses 'lane' without definition.
root_cause: 'Per lane' was used without definition (possibly meaning per module or per aggregate link), and the present-tense verb was applied to a range spanning current and future technology.
correction: Define 'lane' explicitly and scope the tense: e.g., 'optical modules at 400–800 Gb/s aggregate are entering data centers, with per-lane (per-wavelength) rates of 100–200 Gb/s deployed today and 400 Gb/s per lane in development.' Or: 'lane rates of 100–200 Gb/s are deployed, with 400 Gb/s per lane under development and higher rates in research.'
acceptance_test: The term 'lane' is defined, and the claimed rates are consistent with the deployment stage implied by the verb tense.

quoted_clause: How should EP sizing and all-to-all communication be budgeted for frontier MoE models at extreme sparsity? 2026 MoE scaling has moved the specialist/EP frontier: Kimi K3 activates just 16 of 896 routed experts per token (2.8T total / 104B active) via its Stable LatentMoE [1P: arXiv 2607.24653]; Qwen3.8-Flash-Next routes 10+1 of 512 experts (125B total / 6B active) [1P: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next]. This combination — extreme sparsity (16/896 ≈ 1.8% expert activation), the total expert residency that must be sharded *if the deployment keeps all experts resident in HBM* (expert offloading or caching otherwise changes the capacity calculus), and the all-to-all routing EP *can require when experts are distributed across devices* (replicated or cached expert placements avoid it) — is why expert-parallel and fused cross-expert comm kernels (e.g. MoE expert parallelism with fused compute/communication, as in DeepSeek's DeepEP/TileLang infra) are increasingly central to serving large MoE fleets [1P: arXiv 2606.19348]. For the architect this changes the serving calculus: a frontier MoE's activated footprint (Kimi 104B, Qwen 6B) can be dramatically smaller than its total size, so the *compute* decision is made against active parameters — but the *memory-bound* EP decision (how many experts must be resident) is made against **total** parameters when the full expert set must occupy HBM even when only a fraction is routed per token. The activated-vs-total residency crossover at current interconnect bandwidths is unmeasured [UNRESOLVED].
observed: Single ~200-word paragraph containing six distinct intellectual moves: (1) the question, (2) two model examples, (3) a three-factor combination clause with nested parentheticals, (4) a kernel-infrastructure citation, (5) the architect's compute-vs-memory takeaway, (6) the unresolved crossover. The 'This combination — A (...), B (...), and C (...) — is why...' sentence requires holding three conditional sub-clauses inside one sentence before reaching the main verb.
evidence: Reading the paragraph reveals three levels of parenthetical nesting and six distinct intellectual moves in one paragraph. The other three bullets in the same section are each 1–2 sentences.
root_cause: All supporting material for the EP-sizing question was composed as one paragraph rather than split at natural boundaries.
correction: Break into 2–3 paragraphs: (1) question + model examples as context, (2) three-factor combination + kernel citation as why-it-matters, (3) architect's takeaway + unresolved crossover as conclusion. Alternatively, move model-specific details (Kimi/Qwen specs) to a footnote and keep the paragraph focused on the architectural question.
acceptance_test: The MoE/EP bullet reads as 2–3 short paragraphs or has model details in a footnote; no sentence contains more than one level of parenthetical nesting.

quoted_clause: Each strategy is best distinguished by *what it trades bandwidth for*.
observed: The framing implies all strategies trade bandwidth, but inference DP explicitly does not (the very next paragraph says 'inference replicas have no gradient synchronization') and CP's primary trade is memory capacity, not bandwidth.
evidence: The body text immediately contradicts the framing for inference DP. The opening sentence sets an expectation the section then has to correct.
root_cause: Framing sentence written for the training-DP case and not generalized to cover all six strategies.
correction: Broaden the framing, e.g., 'Each strategy is best distinguished by what it trades — bandwidth, memory capacity, or bubbles — and what it gains in return.'
acceptance_test: The opening sentence of Section 2 is consistent with the fact that inference DP involves no bandwidth trade and CP's primary trade is memory capacity.

page_hint: Section 2, Mental Model, resource triangle paragraph
quoted_clause: When a GPU runs out of *memory*, we reach for TP/PP (weight splitting).
observed: The heuristic maps 'memory' to TP/PP only. KV-cache/sequence memory pressure (addressed by CP) is mentioned in the next sentence ('CP addresses long-sequence/KV capacity, not idle-fill') but is not integrated into the initial memory heuristic. Memory has two distinct sources (weights vs. KV/sequence) mapping to different strategies.
evidence: Adjacent sentences discuss weight memory (→ TP/PP) and KV/sequence memory (→ CP) separately without unifying them in the heuristic.
root_cause: Heuristic written for weight memory; CP appended as a separate note rather than integrated.
correction: Revise: 'When *weight* memory binds, we reach for TP/PP; when *KV/sequence* memory binds, we reach for CP.'
acceptance_test: The resource-triangle heuristic explicitly distinguishes weight-memory pressure (→ TP/PP) from KV/sequence-memory pressure (→ CP) in a single sentence or closely coupled pair.

quoted_clause: grad bytes = N_params × bytes/param = 70 × 10⁹ × 4 B ≈ 280 GB
observed: Uses FP32 gradients (4 bytes) without explaining why FP32 rather than FP16/BF16. The text notes the Ch 9 precision difference ('Chapter 9's separate 140 GB example assumes FP16 gradients, so the two examples must retain their different precision bases') but provides no rationale for the FP32 choice here.
evidence: Text explicitly flags the precision difference between chapters but does not justify FP32. In practice, mixed-precision training often uses FP16/BF16 gradients with FP32 master weights; some implementations do use FP32 gradients.
root_cause: FP32 chosen as a conservative communication model; rationale not stated.
correction: Add a brief clause: 'FP32 gradients are used here as a conservative communication model; some implementations sync FP16/BF16 gradients (halving the bytes) with loss scaling or FP32 master weights.'
acceptance_test: The DP gradient example includes a one-clause justification for the FP32 precision choice, and the reader can explain why Ch 9 and Ch 10 use different gradient precisions.

quoted_clause: the pipeline takes m+P-1 stage-time units to complete m·P units of useful work; the P-1 extra units are the fill-and-drain bubble
observed: 'stage-time units' is ambiguous: it could mean pipeline wall-clock time (m+P−1) or total time summed across all stages (P×(m+P−1)). The math is correct only under the pipeline-time reading, but 'stage-time' conventionally suggests per-stage or summed-across-stages time.
evidence: Under pipeline-time: total = m+P−1, bubble = P−1. Under summed-stage-time: total = P(m+P−1), bubble = P(P−1). The text's numbers (m+P−1 and P−1) only work under the pipeline-time reading.
root_cause: Non-standard terminology: 'stage-time units' used where 'pipeline time units' or simply 'time steps' would be unambiguous.
correction: Replace 'stage-time units' with 'pipeline time units' or 'time steps': 'the pipeline takes m+P−1 time steps to complete m·P units of useful work; the P−1 extra steps are the fill-and-drain bubble.'
acceptance_test: The PP bubble explanation uses an unambiguous time unit term; a reader can correctly identify the bubble as P−1 (pipeline time) without guessing.

quoted_clause: Moving the cross-node decomposition from TP to PP cuts TPOT from 80 ms to 35 ms [ILLUSTRATIVE]
observed: 80 − 45 = 35 exactly, implying PP introduces zero additional cost. PP does introduce stage-boundary communication and pipeline bubbles, neither of which is mentioned in the mini-case's cost accounting.
evidence: The chapter's own PP section establishes non-zero bubble cost (72.7% utilization at P=4, m=8). The mini-case's arithmetic (80−45=35) suggests no PP overhead is included.
root_cause: Illustrative numbers chosen for clean arithmetic (80 − 45 = 35) without accounting for PP's own communication and bubble costs.
correction: Either (a) adjust the numbers so 35 ms includes a small PP overhead (e.g., 'cuts TPOT from 80 ms to 38 ms, with 3 ms of PP stage-boundary cost and bubble'), or (b) add a clause acknowledging PP's residual cost: 'cuts TPOT from 80 ms to 35 ms [ILLUSTRATIVE] — the residual includes PP stage-boundary transfers and a small bubble, both far cheaper than per-layer cross-node all-reduce.'
acceptance_test: The mini-case's TP→PP transition either includes PP's communication/bubble cost in the new TPOT or explicitly acknowledges that the illustrative numbers abstract it away.

page_hint: Section 1 (Communication-specificity note) vs Section 3 (PP subsection) vs Section 8 (mini-case)
quoted_clause: more microbatches shrink the bubble but add memory (Section 1) vs With P stages and m micro-batches (Section 3) vs micro-batch count m (Section 8)
observed: Both 'microbatch' (no hyphen) and 'micro-batch' (hyphenated) are used for the same concept within the chapter.
evidence: Section 1: 'microbatches'. Section 3: 'micro-batches'. Section 8: 'micro-batch'.
root_cause: Inconsistent hyphenation across sections, likely from different drafting passes.
correction: Standardize on one form throughout the chapter (and ideally the book). 'micro-batch' appears more frequently in this chapter (2 occurrences vs 1 for 'microbatch').
acceptance_test: A grep for 'microbatch' and 'micro-batch' in the chapter source returns only one spelling.

page_hint: §3, 'When to Disaggregate: Prefill and Decode Want Different Pools'
quoted_clause: prefill is **compute-bound** — compute-dominated there, a regime statement not a law (Ch 2) (~1.29 PFLOP → ~1.19 PFLOPS required over the ~1.08 s prefill budget, vs 0.989 PFLOPS peak on a single H100; under the canonical 8xH100 TP=8 host the same prefill is ~0.16 PFLOP per GPU and takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU (Ch 12), so the single-device figure describes a one-GPU deployment, not the canonical host), decode is **bandwidth-bound** (arithmetic intensity = B FLOP/byte for FP16 weights: ~1.0 at batch 1, ~17.5 at the canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point (Ch 4 §6 / Ch 7 / Ch 17; 436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB = KV budget ÷ per-request KV) — both far below the H100 ridge of ~295 FLOP/byte, so bandwidth binds; the whole-model weight-read rate is ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU, sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU under the canonical 8×H100 host, Ch 6)
observed: A single ~150-word sentence contains four or more levels of nested parentheticals carrying two independent derivations (prefill FLOP budget and decode arithmetic-intensity/weight-read-rate), six cross-references, and two regime qualifications. The reader must hold the main claim (prefill compute-bound, decode bandwidth-bound) in working memory while parsing deeply nested derivations and qualifications.
evidence: All arithmetic within the sentence is independently correct: 2×70e9×9200=1.288 PFLOP≈1.29; 1.29/1.08≈1.19 PFLOPS; 1.29/8≈0.161 PFLOP; 0.161/(0.989×0.35)≈0.465≈0.47 s; AI at B=1 is 1.0, at B=17.5 is 17.5; 436/24.9=17.51; ridge=989/3350≈295; 140×40=5600 GB/s=5.6 TB/s; 5.6/8=0.70. The problem is purely presentational: the nesting depth makes correct content unnecessarily hard to parse.
root_cause: Two independent derivations (prefill and decode) were compressed into one sentence with parenthetical embedding rather than separated into distinct sentences or a short derivation block.
correction: Restructure into: (1) a short topic sentence stating both regime claims with the Ch 2 qualification; (2) a prefill derivation sentence or two; (3) a decode derivation sentence or two. Keep cross-references but reduce nesting to at most one level per sentence. Example skeleton: 'At the canonical operating point, prefill is compute-bound and decode is bandwidth-bound — both regime statements, not laws (Ch 2). Prefill: ~1.29 PFLOP over the ~1.08 s budget requires ~1.19 PFLOPS, above a single H100's 0.989 PFLOPS peak; on the canonical 8×H100 TP=8 host the per-GPU share is ~0.16 PFLOP, completed in ~0.47 s at 35% MFU (Ch 12). Decode: weight-read arithmetic intensity is B FLOP/byte for FP16 — ~1.0 at batch 1, ~17.5 at the canonical ~17.5-concurrent operating point (436 GB ÷ 24.9 GB; Ch 4 §6 / Ch 7 / Ch 17) — both far below the H100 ridge of ~295 FLOP/byte, so bandwidth binds. The whole-model weight-read rate is ~5.6 TB/s at batch 1 (Ch 6), sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU on the canonical host.'
acceptance_test: The restructured passage contains no sentence with more than two levels of parenthetical nesting; all numerical values and cross-references are preserved; a reader can identify both regime claims and both derivations within one pass.

quoted_clause: | Technique | Mechanism | Primary resource traded | When it matters | Source |
observed: The column header 'Primary resource traded' does not accurately describe the column content for all rows. For PagedAttention ('memory capacity') and prefix caching ('prefill FLOPs + memory') a genuine trade is described. For continuous batching ('compute+bandwidth util') the entry describes a resource whose utilization improves, not something traded away. For discrete batching ('slot occupancy (wastes capacity)') the entry describes waste, not a trade. For P/D disaggregation ('both at scale') the entry is ambiguous about what is given up.
evidence: Row-by-row inspection of Table 11-1 against the column header. The header implies a give-up/get relationship (you trade X for Y), but the entries inconsistently represent: resources improved, resources wasted, resources leveraged, and resources managed.
root_cause: The column header was chosen to fit some rows but not all; the underlying concept varies by mechanism (some mechanisms trade, some improve utilization, some reduce waste).
correction: Rename the column to 'Primary resource lever' or 'Resource affected', which accurately covers all five rows: discrete batching wastes slot occupancy; continuous batching leverages compute+bandwidth utilization; PagedAttention leverages memory capacity; prefix caching leverages prefill FLOPs and memory; P/D disaggregation leverages both at scale. Alternatively, keep 'traded' and rewrite the continuous-batching and discrete-batching entries to describe an actual trade (e.g., continuous batching: 'scheduling complexity for utilization').
acceptance_test: Every row's entry in the renamed column accurately describes what the header claims, without requiring the reader to reinterpret the header per row.

quoted_clause: The KV moves once per request, then stays local (ownership splits); the split itself exists because the two stages want opposite resources under load — prefill needs compute capacity (per-request ~1.19 PFLOPS over the ~1.08 s prefill budget vs 0.989 peak single-H100; on the canonical 8×H100 host the same prefill takes ~0.47 s at 35% MFU, Ch 12), while decode needs HBM bandwidth (at batch size 1 and 25 ms TPOT — 40 tokens/s — the whole-model weight-read rate of ~5.6 TB/s if served by one device vs 3.35 TB/s per GPU, sharded to ~0.70 TB/s per GPU under the canonical 8×H100 host, Ch 6; batching divides the rate proportionally) [1P][DERIVED].
observed: The figure caption contains approximately 100 words of dense numerical derivation (prefill FLOP budget, MFU, weight-read rate, per-GPU sharding) that duplicates content already present in the body text of §3 'When to Disaggregate'. A reader encountering the figure receives a wall of numbers before processing the visual.
evidence: The same derivations (1.19 PFLOPS / 1.08 s / 0.989 peak / 0.47 s at 35% MFU / 5.6 TB/s / 3.35 TB/s / 0.70 TB/s) appear in both the body paragraph and the caption. The caption's primary job — telling the reader what to learn from the figure — is buried under derivation content that belongs in body text or Note 11.3-1.
root_cause: The caption was used as a location for the full derivation rather than a pointer to the body text's derivation.
correction: Shorten the caption to state the figure's key insight (e.g., 'The KV moves once per request, then stays local; the split exists because prefill needs compute capacity while decode needs HBM bandwidth — see §3 and Note 11.3-1 for the derivations.') and move any unique numerical content not already in the body into Note 11.3-1 or the body text.
acceptance_test: The caption is under ~40 words, states what the reader should learn from the figure, and does not duplicate numerical derivations already present in the body text.

page_hint: §6, 'What the capability table does not promise'
quoted_clause: ### What the capability table does not promise
observed: This section (~500 words) covers two distinct topics without clear internal separation: (a) qualifying the capability table (quantization support ≠ end-to-end support, deployment record requirements) and (b) introducing serving qualification for diverse model classes (diffusion language models, adaptive depth, early exit, seven-gate record). The transition from (a) to (b) occurs at 'A serving feature belongs to an algorithm path' but is not marked by a subheading or explicit signpost, so the reader may lose track of the section's original purpose (qualifying Table 11-2).
evidence: The section opens by referencing the capability table, then pivots to diffusion schedulers, refinement rounds, FDFO scheduling, adaptive depth, depth distributions, and economic denominators — topics that go well beyond qualifying a table. The seven-gate qualification record at the end is a standalone framework that could serve as its own subsection.
root_cause: Two related but distinct pedagogical goals (table qualification and model-class qualification) were merged into one section without structural markers.
correction: Add an intermediate subheading (e.g., '#### Serving qualification for diverse model classes') at the pivot point 'A serving feature belongs to an algorithm path', or split into two subsections: one for table qualification and one for model-class qualification with the seven-gate record as a concluding framework.
acceptance_test: A reader can identify the section's two main topics from the headings alone, and the transition between them is explicitly marked.

quoted_clause: under the canonical 8xH100 TP=8 host
observed: Uses lowercase 'x' in '8xH100' while the same paragraph and the rest of the chapter use the multiplication sign '×' in '8×H100' (e.g., 'under the canonical 8×H100 host', 'on the canonical 8×H100 host', 'one 8×H100 replica').
evidence: Direct comparison of the two spellings within §3 and across the chapter.
root_cause: Typographic inconsistency during editing.
correction: Change '8xH100' to '8×H100' for consistency with the rest of the chapter.

quoted_clause: at the replica's admitted load (≈1.3-2 req/s per Ch 14 Step 3)
observed: Uses a hyphen '-' for the numeric range '1.3-2' while §3 uses an en-dash '–' for the same range: 'per-host ≈1.3–2 req/s'.

quoted_clause: The batch is locked until its *slowest* member finishes (fits-all-in-one-run)
observed: The parenthetical '(fits-all-in-one-run)' is awkward compound-adjective phrasing that is not standard terminology and could confuse readers. It appears to mean 'all requests fit in one run/batch' but the hyphenation makes it read as a single compound modifier.
evidence: The phrase does not appear elsewhere in the chapter and is not defined. Standard terminology for this behavior is 'run-to-completion' or simply 'the batch runs to completion'.
root_cause: Non-standard coinage used as a parenthetical gloss.
correction: Replace with a standard phrase: '(the batch runs to completion)' or simply remove the parenthetical, since the preceding clause 'locked until its slowest member finishes' already conveys the meaning.
acceptance_test: The parenthetical is either removed or replaced with a standard, self-explanatory phrase.

quoted_clause: idle bubbles at the end of every batch
observed: The phrase 'idle bubbles' could be misread as GPU idleness, but in context it refers to batch-slot idleness (finished requests leave empty slots while the longest request continues). The GPU is still doing work — just with a reduced effective batch size. The next bullet ('the GPU drains (no work) then floods') correctly describes actual GPU idleness between batches, creating a potential confusion between the two types of idleness.
evidence: In discrete batching, when short outputs finish, their slots become empty but the GPU continues processing the longest request. The GPU is not idle; the batch is underutilized. The phrase 'idle bubbles at the end of every batch' is ambiguous between slot-level and GPU-level idleness.
root_cause: Imprecise wording that conflates slot idleness with GPU idleness.
correction: Clarify: 'empty trailing slots reduce the effective batch size while the longest request finishes' or 'the batch shrinks as short outputs complete, reducing utilization'.
acceptance_test: The sentence unambiguously describes slot-level underutilization (not GPU idleness) during the trailing phase of a batch.

quoted_clause: The four are independent dials — mechanisms can be combined in principle, subject to implementation support and resource interactions
observed: The word 'independent' in 'independent dials' suggests the four mechanisms do not affect each other, but the immediately following clause acknowledges 'resource interactions' (e.g., prefix caching and continuous batching drawing on the same KV pool). The figure title uses 'separable concerns, not a stack' — 'separable' is the more accurate term (addressable in any order) while 'independent' overstates the claim.
evidence: The figure title says 'separable' and the description says 'independent'; these are different claims. Separable = can be addressed in any order. Independent = do not affect each other. The text's own parenthetical example (shared KV pool) demonstrates they are not independent.
root_cause: Word choice drift between figure title ('separable') and figure description ('independent').
correction: Change 'independent dials' to 'separable dials' or 'independently addressable dials' to match the figure title and the acknowledged resource interactions.
acceptance_test: The figure description uses 'separable' or an equivalent term consistent with the figure title and the acknowledged interactions.

quoted_clause: Bigger discrete batches raise raw tokens/s but push TTFT past the SLO, zeroing goodput (Ch6).
observed: 'Zeroing goodput' reads as 'goodput becomes zero' (all requests miss the SLO), which is stronger than the evidence supports. In practice, larger batches increase average TTFT and cause more requests to miss the SLO, reducing goodput — but not necessarily reducing it to zero. Some requests may still meet the SLO.
evidence: Goodput is defined as tokens/s arriving before the SLO deadline (§4). Larger batches push the TTFT distribution rightward; requests in the left tail may still meet the 2 s p95 SLO. 'Zeroing' implies the entire goodput contribution is eliminated.
root_cause: Hyperbolic phrasing in a common-mistakes bullet that overstates the consequence.
correction: Replace 'zeroing goodput' with 'collapsing goodput' or 'driving goodput toward zero as more requests miss the SLO deadline'.
acceptance_test: The corrected phrasing does not imply goodput reaches exactly zero, while still conveying that goodput degrades severely.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (worked example) and Ch 13 §3 (placing the canonical workload); also Table 12-1 footnote
quoted_clause: The KV cache for 9.2K context at FP16 precision ... approximately 24 GB ... [Ch 13] KV for the 9.5K max context at FP16 ≈ 24.9 GB; inference residency ≈ 165 GB
observed: Ch 12 computes KV at 9.2K context (input only) giving ~24 GB and total residency 164 GB. Ch 13 computes KV at 9.5K context (input + output) giving ~24.9 GB and total residency ~165 GB. The capacity screen used throughout (17.5 requests/host = floor(436/24.9)) is based on the 9.5K figure. Table 12-1 notes the numerical difference ('Ch 13's 9.5K basis gives ~165 GB') but never explains WHY the bases differ. A reader deriving 17.5 from Ch 12's 24 GB figure gets 436/24 = 18.2, not 17.5.
evidence: 436/24 = 18.17 vs 436/24.9 = 17.51. The 17-slot floor used in all host-count arithmetic (Ch 12 §3, Ch 13 §3, Ch 13 §8) comes from the 9.5K basis, but Ch 12's worked example only establishes the 9.2K basis.
root_cause: Two different context-length bases (input-only 9.2K vs input+output 9.5K) are used for KV sizing across chapters without a conceptual explanation of when each is appropriate. The Table 12-1 footnote flags the number but not the reason.
correction: Add one sentence in Ch 12 §3 or §4 explaining that prefill-time KV covers the 9.2K input while maximum per-request KV (used for concurrency/capacity screens) covers 9.5K (input + output), and that the 17-slot figure derives from the 9.5K basis. Alternatively, use 9.5K consistently in Ch 12's worked example and note that prefill-time KV is slightly smaller.
acceptance_test: A reader can derive 17.5 slots/host from numbers presented in Ch 12 alone, or Ch 12 explicitly states which basis the 17-slot figure uses and why.

quoted_clause: the gate closes only when the host class is replicated to ~5 hosts on the average prefill screen (92K ÷ 19.8K ≈ 4.65 → 5), ~6 on the average KV/service-time screen (10 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 5.06 → 6), and ~21 at peak (40 × 8.6 ÷ 17 ≈ 20.2 → 21) (Chs. 15–17)
observed: The numbers 17 (KV slots per host) and 8.6 s (service time) are used in Ch 12's host-count arithmetic without being derived or restated in Ch 12. The cross-reference '(Chs. 15–17)' points forward, not to where these numbers are established. The reader encountering Ch 12 cannot verify these calculations without external chapters.
evidence: 17 = floor(436/24.9) = floor(17.51); 8.6 s is referenced as 'canonical' but its derivation is not in this chapter. Ch 12 derives 436 GB ('640 − 140 weights − ~64 runtime ≈ 436 GB, Ch 7/17') but stops there.
root_cause: Key inputs to the host-count formula are established in earlier chapters but not restated or briefly derived where they are first used in arithmetic.
correction: Add a parenthetical in Ch 12 §3 at the first use: e.g., '(17 = floor of the 436 GB KV budget ÷ 24.9 GB per-request KV at 9.5K; 8.6 s = the canonical service time from Ch 7)'. This costs one line and makes the arithmetic self-contained.
acceptance_test: A reader can follow the host-count arithmetic in Ch 12 §3 without leaving the chapter to look up 17 or 8.6.

page_hint: Ch 13 §2 (Mental Model), bullet list under 'classic triggers for climbing'
quoted_clause: Latency/geography: SLO can't be met due to distance or contention → split prefill/decode (a within-tier move).
observed: This bullet is listed under 'The classic triggers for climbing' but its stated response ('split prefill/decode') is explicitly labeled 'a within-tier move' — i.e., NOT a climb. The first three bullets all describe responses that involve climbing to a higher tier; this one does not. The structure implies trigger → climb, but this bullet breaks that pattern without explanation.
evidence: Bullets 1–3: Memory → cluster (climb); KV residency → single host (climb from Local to Server); Traffic → cluster (climb). Bullet 4: Latency/geography → within-tier move (no climb). The section header says 'triggers for climbing'.
root_cause: The bullet conflates a trigger (latency/geography problem) with a response that happens to be within-tier, placed in a list whose other entries all produce tier escalation.
correction: Either (a) move this bullet out of the 'triggers for climbing' list into a separate note about within-tier responses to latency problems, or (b) restructure it to show that latency/geography can trigger either a within-tier response (P/D disaggregation) or a placement response (moving closer, which is de-escalation), making clear which is a climb and which is not.
acceptance_test: Every bullet under 'triggers for climbing' describes a response that actually climbs a tier, or the section explicitly notes which bullets describe within-tier responses.

quoted_clause: KV residency per GPU: model + KV no longer fits one GPU → single host — the within-tier step Fig 13.1 shows between Single GPU and Single host.
observed: Single GPU = Local/edge tier; Single host = Server tier (per the Fig 13.1 caption: 'Single GPU = Local/edge, Single host = Server'). These are DIFFERENT tiers. Calling the step between them 'within-tier' is incorrect or at minimum deeply confusing.
evidence: Fig 13.1 caption explicitly maps: Single GPU = Local/edge, Single host = Server, Multi-host = Cluster, Cluster/fleet = Hyperscale fleet. The step from Single GPU to Single host crosses the Local/edge → Server boundary.
root_cause: The term 'within-tier' is used where 'inter-tier' or 'up one rung' is meant, or the author considers Local/edge and Server to be 'within' the same broad category — but the chapter's own tier definitions say otherwise.
correction: Replace 'within-tier step' with 'one-rung step' or 'inter-tier step (Local/edge → Server)' to match the chapter's own tier definitions.
acceptance_test: The terminology for the Single GPU → Single host transition is consistent with the four-tier definitions in §13.1 and the Fig 13.1 caption.

quoted_clause: a bounded set of two to three candidates, each designed to probe a distinct gate — memory fit, throughput, or quality
observed: The claim says each candidate probes a distinct gate from the set {memory fit, throughput, quality}. The actual candidates: (a) open gate = throughput; (b) open gate = throughput at single prefill host; (c) open gate = quality. No candidate has memory fit as its open gate. (a) and (b) probe the same gate (throughput). The claim of three distinct gates probed by three candidates is not realized.
evidence: Open-gate table in Ch 12: (a) throughput open; (b) throughput open at a single prefill host; (c) quality open. Memory fit passes for all three candidates (164 < 640, 164 < 640, 15 < 80).
root_cause: The opening paragraph promises a one-to-one mapping between candidates and gates, but the worked example produces two throughput-probing candidates and one quality-probing candidate, with memory fit never binding.
correction: Either (a) revise the claim to 'each designed to probe a different aspect of the constraint set — single-host throughput, phase-split throughput, or quality-vs-size' or (b) add a fourth candidate where memory fit is the binding constraint (e.g., a model that barely fits one host, forcing a memory-driven design choice), or (c) soften to 'each designed to stress-test the gates from a different angle'.
acceptance_test: The opening claim about distinct gates matches the actual open-gate distribution of the candidates presented in §12.3.

page_hint: Ch 12 §3 (candidate a description) vs Table 12-1 vs unnumbered open-gate table

page_hint: Ch 13 §3 (Escalating: When 10× Traffic Forces the Cluster Tier)
quoted_clause: At ~100 rps × 9.5K tokens = ~950K tokens/s, one host's goodput is exceeded.
observed: The 950K figure uses total tokens per request (9.5K = 9.2K input + 300 output), but the subsequent host-count calculation uses the KV/service-time screen (based on 8.6 s service time and 17 slots), not a total-tokens/s comparison. The prefill screen elsewhere uses 9.2K input tokens (920K input tokens/s at 100 rps). The 950K figure is not used in any calculation and mixes total-token demand with a discussion of prefill capacity.
evidence: 100 × 9,500 = 950,000 (total tokens). 100 × 9,200 = 920,000 (input tokens). The host count uses ⌈100 × 8.6 / 17⌉ = 51, which is a KV/service-time screen, not a tokens/s screen. The 950K number appears only as an illustrative magnitude.
root_cause: The text uses total tokens to establish that one host is insufficient, but the metric doesn't match the screen that follows, and the number isn't used downstream.
correction: Either use input tokens consistently ('~920K input tokens/s, far above one host's ~19.8K prefill ceiling') or explicitly note that 950K is total-token demand shown for magnitude while the host count uses the KV/service-time screen.
acceptance_test: The token-demand figure in the escalation paragraph matches the metric used in the subsequent host-count calculation, or the mismatch is explicitly noted.

quoted_clause: continuous batching on 8×H100 at ~9.5K tokens/request sustained roughly tens of thousands of tokens/s
observed: 'Tens of thousands of tokens/s' is vague and does not specify whether this refers to prefill tokens/s (~19.8K), decode tokens/s, or total tokens/s. The surrounding context discusses prefill capacity, but the phrase could be read as total throughput.
evidence: Ch 12 establishes ~19,800 prefill-tokens/s for the 70B on 8×H100. The phrase 'tens of thousands' is consistent with this but doesn't specify the metric.
root_cause: Deliberate vagueness in a conceptual discussion, but the vagueness obscures which resource is being discussed.
correction: Replace with 'sustained roughly ~20K prefill-tokens/s (Ch 8)' or 'roughly tens of thousands of prefill-tokens/s' to specify the metric.
acceptance_test: The throughput figure in the escalation paragraph specifies prefill vs decode vs total.

quoted_clause: 24,725 exact: 989 TFLOP/s × 35% MFU ÷ 14 GFLOP/token
observed: The word 'exact' is used for 24,725, but the inputs are approximate: 989 TFLOPS is a vendor spec (dense FP16), 35% MFU is an assumption, and 14 GFLOP/token is a first-order approximation (2 × 7B, ignoring attention quadratic term and other details). The calculation is exact GIVEN the inputs, but the inputs are not exact.
evidence: 989 × 10^12 × 0.35 / (14 × 10^9) = 24,725. But 14 GFLOP/token for a 7B model is approximate (actual depends on architecture, attention heads, etc.), and 35% MFU is an assumption.
root_cause: 'Exact' conflates arithmetic precision with input precision.
correction: Replace 'exact' with '24,725 (from the stated inputs)' or '~24,725' to match the tilde used for the comparable 70B figure (~2,472).
acceptance_test: Numbers derived from approximate inputs are not labeled 'exact'.

page_hint: Ch 12 Table 12-2 (Monthly fully loaded cost row) and §12.8

page_hint: Ch 13 §2 (Mental Model), fourth bullet; also Ch 13 §3
quoted_clause: split prefill/decode (a within-tier move)
observed: P/D disaggregation is described as 'a within-tier move'. However, P/D disaggregation typically requires two separate host pools (prefill pool + decode pool), which at the Server tier (1-8 GPUs per host) could mean two 8×H100 hosts = 16 GPUs total. Whether this remains 'within-tier' depends on whether the tier is defined per-host or per-deployment. The chapter's tier definitions are per-deployment ('Server — one host with 1-8 GPUs'), so two hosts for P/D would be a Cluster-tier deployment.
evidence: §13.1: 'Server — one host with 1-8 GPUs'. P/D disaggregation requires at minimum two hosts (prefill + decode pools). Two hosts = multiple hosts = Cluster tier per §13.1.
root_cause: The 'within-tier' label for P/D disaggregation conflicts with the chapter's own tier definitions when P/D requires multiple hosts.
correction: Qualify the claim: 'split prefill/decode (a within-tier move if both pools fit one host; a cluster-tier move if they require separate hosts)' or clarify that the tier is defined per-model-residency, not per-deployment.
acceptance_test: The tier classification of P/D disaggregation is consistent with the chapter's tier definitions.
